newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar slips as speculators move in.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar slips as speculators move in.

text.p: The Singapore dollar continued to head south against its U.S. counterpart on Tuesday largely on the back of sales by U.S. funds, blamed for the recent sell-off in regional currencies, dealers said.
"The funds are trying to attack all the currencies in the region," a dealer with a U.S. bank in Singapore said.
He said the rest of the market was mostly squared up in the Singapore dollar but U.S. funds were still extending their long dollar/Sing positions.
The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4386/96 to the U.S. dollar at 0820 GMT against its opening 1.4358. It briefly hit a low of 1.4405 on selling from London-based parties.
The domestic currency has been under siege since late last week after Thailand's shock move towards a managed float exchange rate system.
Dealers said large U.S. funds, which had bet on a devaluation of the Thai baht, were turning on other Southeast Asian currencies to test how far they could be pushed.
"I think dollar/Sing can go to its last high of 1.4500/20," the U.S. bank dealer said.
He added that most players were not afraid of intervention by the de facto central bank ahead of that level, unless the Singapore dollar moved sharply.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) typically intervenes to stem sudden movements in the domestic currency.

Jacqueline Ong, economist at research firm I.D.E.A., said the Singapore dollar's traditional "safe haven" status among regional currencies could have undergone a slight shift with Singapore authorities endorsing a more modest appreciation of the unit.

"In the past, we've always assumed a strong Sing dollar policy from the government. But recently (Finance Minister) Richard Hu said there's no need for the Sing dollar to appreciate that much if inflation stays under control," Ong said.
"To the extent that foreign inflationary pressures become more muted, our exchange rate does not have to appreciate as much as it did before," Hu said in a speech in March.
Ong said players were unlikely to go aggressively into the Singapore dollar despite regional uncertainties due to a belief the MAS would intervene to prevent its sharp rise.
"Although we're sure now that the local authorities don't want the Sing dollar to be strengthening so fast, they definitely do not want it to weaken to like 1.45 overnight," she said.
She said a gradual move in the Singapore dollar towards 1.45 would probably be acceptable to local authorities, as long as the U.S. dollar also strengthened towards 115 yen.
